text: This chapter teaches the harmonic vocabulary and improvisational toolkit for "Sweet Georgia Brown," establishing the VI7 dominant substitution rule -- that diatonic minor chords can be raised to dominant 7ths -- and demonstrating how this single principle generates the song's entire harmonic architecture, from the opening A-section cycle of dominant 7ths resolving in fourths, through the relative minor key transition to F minor, to the descending chromatic dominant approach that defines the "backdoor" I7-VI7-ii-V-I cadential pattern in bars 29-32. The chapter reframes scales as pitch collections rather than mechanical exercises, introducing the Mixolydian scale (major scale with a b7, or the 5th mode of major) as the primary melodic resource over dominant 7 chords, and provides a concrete chord-tone pattern exercise that maps Mixolydian note choices onto the cycling changes. Greenan's characteristic move here is the analytical labeling of common structural patterns -- particularly "backdoor" as a reusable shorthand -- and the insistence on transposing all licks through 12 keys as a non-negotiable practice principle, bridging micro-level phrase work with macro-level compositional understanding.
